title: Baba Ganoush
subtitle: Smoky charred aubergine dip
excerpt: Aubergines charred directly over a flame until the skin is burnt and blistered and the flesh inside has collapsed to smoky, yielding mush, then blended with tahini, garlic, and lemon juice. The smoke from the charring is the whole point.

recipe.sourceNotes: Baba ganoush (also spelled ganouj or ghanouj) is eaten across the Levant, Egypt, and other parts of the Middle East, with the name likely deriving from Arabic meaning pampered daddy or similar affectionate terms. The defining technique is the open-flame charring of the whole aubergine; this is not the same as grilling or roasting in an oven. The direct contact with flame produces deep charring on the skin that permeates the flesh with a distinctive smoky flavour that cannot be replicated any other way. Tahini (sesame paste), garlic, and lemon juice are the standard additions across the Levantine version; some Egyptian versions omit tahini entirely. The dish is served at room temperature with pitta bread or vegetables.

content.text: Char the aubergine directly on a gas flame or very close under a grill, turning regularly with tongs. It must be completely blackened on the outside and completely collapsed inside. A pale, partially cooked aubergine will produce a flat, bitter dip with no smoke character. The black, papery skin is easy to peel once the aubergine has cooled.

Pierce each aubergine a few times with a knife. Place directly on a gas flame at medium-high heat, or as close as possible under a very hot grill. Cook for 20 to 30 minutes, turning with tongs every 5 minutes, until completely blackened all over and entirely soft and collapsed when pressed.

Transfer to a colander over a bowl and leave to cool for 15 minutes. Peel away and discard the charred skin; this should come off easily. If any small charred bits remain, leave them as they add flavour.

Roughly chop or mash the aubergine flesh; do not blend to a smooth paste unless you prefer a smoother texture. Mix in the garlic, lemon juice, olive oil, and salt. Taste and adjust. Serve on a plate, drizzled with more olive oil and scattered with parsley and paprika, with warm pitta bread.
